purpose: Trientine is used to treat Wilson's disease, a rare inherited condition where too much copper builds up in your body. It helps remove the extra copper so it doesn't damage your liver, brain, and other organs. It is typically used in people who cannot tolerate penicillamine, another copper-removing medicine.
how_it_works: Your body normally gets rid of excess copper on its own, but in Wilson's disease it cannot do that properly. Trientine works by latching onto the extra copper in your body and binding to it tightly. Once bound, the copper is carried out of your body through your urine, lowering the levels to a safer range.
common_side_effects: Some people notice stomach upset, nausea, or heartburn. You may also experience muscle or joint pain, skin rash, or a general feeling of tiredness. Iron levels in your blood can drop over time, so your doctor will monitor this.
warnings: Do not take iron supplements or other mineral supplements at the same time as trientine, as they can block the medicine from working — space them at least 2 hours apart. Tell your doctor right away if you develop fever, swollen glands, or unusual bruising, as these could be signs of a serious reaction. Pregnant women should discuss risks carefully with their doctor. Regular blood and urine tests are needed to make sure the medicine is working safely.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 750 mg to 1,250 mg per day, divided into 2 to 4 doses taken on an empty stomach, at least one hour before or two hours after meals. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on your copper levels and how you respond to treatment. Always swallow capsules whole and follow your doctor's exact instructions.
